Tesla Model Lineup 2026: Complete Guide | Recharged

Tesla’s 2026 model lineup looks very different than it did just a few years ago. In this complete 2026 Tesla model lineup guide, we’ll walk through what’s actually in production, what’s been retired or delayed, and how the shifting product plan should shape your decision to buy a new or used Tesla.

### 2026 Tesla lineup in one sentence

In 2026, Tesla’s real-world lineup is centered on the Model 3 sedan, Model Y SUV and Cybertruck pickup, with the legacy Model S and X gone and the long-promised Roadster still more of a halo project than a mainstream option.

## Overview: Tesla’s 2026 lineup at a glance

### Tesla’s 2026 lineup snapshot

3

Core models

Model 3, Model Y and Cybertruck are Tesla’s volume products in 2026.

250–330 mi

Typical EPA range

Most 2026 Teslas land in this usable, competitive range window.

$40k–$90k

Price span

Approximate new MSRPs across the 2026 Tesla range in the U.S.

250 kW+

Fast charging

Most trims support high DC fast‑charge rates on the Supercharger network.

For 2026, you can think of Tesla’s lineup in three buckets: mainstream daily drivers (Model 3 and Y), lifestyle halo truck (Cybertruck), and the still‑pending Roadster. Meanwhile, the long‑running Model S and Model X have been officially retired, and Tesla’s much‑teased low‑cost “Model 2” style car has been canceled in favor of a still‑evolving next‑generation small EV program.

## What’s changed by 2026: winners, exits, and delays

### Key shifts in Tesla’s lineup heading into 2026

What’s new, what’s gone, and what’s still a question mark

#### Model 3 & Y refreshed

Tesla’s bestsellers get incremental hardware and software updates, with cleaner styling, improved ride comfort, and efficiency tweaks that stretch range without massive battery changes.

#### Cybertruck ramps globally

Cybertruck production continues to scale after its late‑2023 launch, with more configurations and broader market availability by 2026, though supply can still be tight and pricing volatile.

#### Roadster & “cheap Tesla” delayed

The second‑gen Roadster is still not a regular showroom product in 2026, and Tesla’s original $25,000 “Model 2” plan has been walked back in favor of a new small‑EV concept on its next‑gen platform.

### Model S and Model X: Era officially over

By early 2026, Elon Musk publicly acknowledged that Model S and Model X production has ended. If you want one, you’re shopping used, and you should scrutinize battery health and software support closely.

## 2026 Tesla Model 3: The updated compact sedan

### Positioning

The 2026 Tesla Model 3 remains Tesla’s entry sedan and the most efficient car in the lineup. With the recent refresh, it leans into a more premium, minimalist feel inside while holding the line on price and range compared with earlier years.

If you mostly drive solo or as a couple, and you care more about efficiency than cargo volume, the Model 3 still makes more sense than a Model Y.

### Typical 2026 trims

- Model 3 RWD – Single‑motor rear‑drive, the affordability play with solid range.
- Model 3 Long Range – Dual‑motor AWD, more power, more range, and better all‑weather confidence.
- Model 3 Performance – Track‑quick acceleration with uprated brakes and suspension, but some efficiency trade‑off.

### 2026 Model 3: Approximate specs overview

Ballpark numbers; exact figures vary by wheel choice, options and future OTA updates.

| Trim | Drivetrain | EPA range (est.) | 0–60 mph (est.) | Use case |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Model 3 RWD | RWD | ~270 mi | ~5.8 s | Efficient commuter with lower upfront cost |
| Model 3 Long Range | AWD | ~320 mi | ~4.2 s | One‑car household, frequent road trips |
| Model 3 Performance | AWD | ~290 mi | ~3.0 s | Performance‑focused daily driver |

Use this as a directional guide, not a replacement for the official Tesla configurator.

### Used Model 3 sweet spot

For value, look at late‑2021 through refreshed 2024–2025 Model 3 Long Range cars. You often get nearly the same real‑world experience as a 2026 build at a meaningfully lower price, especially once early depreciation has hit.

## 2026 Tesla Model Y: The volume leader SUV

Model Y remains the core of Tesla’s lineup in 2026, with Model 3 and Cybertruck flanking it in price and capability.

If you look at registration data and loan books, the Model Y is the backbone of Tesla’s 2026 business. It combines the Model 3’s basic platform with a more practical hatchback body, higher seating position and family‑friendly cargo space. Tesla has continued refining the ride and cabin in recent updates, making it feel more like a modern crossover and less like an overgrown compact.

### 2026 Model Y: Who each trim is for

Match your driving pattern to the right version

#### Model Y RWD / base AWD

Best for: Price‑sensitive buyers who mostly drive in town or on moderate‑length trips.

Range is still ample for U.S. commuting, and you avoid the steepest part of the price curve.

#### Model Y Long Range

Best for: Families and one‑car households.

Extra range headroom makes winter, mountain and road‑trip driving less stressful.

#### Model Y Performance

Best for: Drivers who want crossover practicality with sports‑sedan acceleration.

Big wheels and stiffer suspension sharpen handling but can reduce comfort and efficiency.

### Why used Model Y demand stays strong

Because the Model Y hits the sweet spot of price, space and range, used Model Ys hold value better than many EVs. That’s good if you already own one; as a buyer, you should focus even more on getting objective battery‑health data and fair‑market pricing instead of just chasing the lowest advertised number.

## 2026 Tesla Cybertruck: Electric pickup with trade-offs

The Cybertruck is the most polarizing piece of Tesla’s 2026 lineup. It’s a stainless‑steel, wedge‑shaped full‑size pickup with serious performance and off‑road capability, but also compromises in bed design, aero drag, efficiency and repairability compared with more conventional unibody EV trucks.

### Where Cybertruck makes sense

- You want an attention‑grabbing halo vehicle with extreme acceleration and unique styling.
- You’ll actually use the tow rating or off‑road capability, not just commute.
- You live near Superchargers that can handle the truck’s high‑power charging and footprint.

### Where it doesn’t

- You just need an efficient family vehicle, a Model Y or Model 3 will be cheaper to buy and run.
- You’re sensitive to ride quality, tire costs or insurance premiums.
- You’re counting on body repairs being straightforward and inexpensive.

### Range vs towing and speed

Like every truck, Cybertruck’s real‑world range drops hard with towing, big wheels or high‑speed driving. If you’re planning long‑distance towing, treat the EPA number as a best‑case scenario and mentally cut it roughly in half.

## Tesla Roadster in 2026: Halo car or vaporware?

Tesla unveiled the second‑generation Roadster back in 2017 as a four‑seat, 200+ mph super‑EV with outrageous acceleration claims. Over the years, timelines have slipped repeatedly. Even with promises of production in the 2024–2025 window, by 2026 the Roadster remains largely theoretical for normal buyers rather than a volume product you can order and drive away.

- If it does arrive in limited numbers, expect pricing deep into supercar territory, not mainstream EV money.
- It’s more about brand halo and engineering spectacle than about solving daily transportation needs.
- For almost everyone, a Model 3 Performance or a well‑spec’d Model Y offers 90% of the usable performance for a fraction of the cost.

### How to think about Roadster

Treat the Roadster as a tech demo and collectors’ item. If you’re mapping out realistic 2026 buying plans, it shouldn’t be on your shortlist unless you’re cross‑shopping Ferraris and McLarens.

## Software, Autopilot/FSD and feature changes for 2026

Tesla’s software strategy in 2026 is shifting. Basic driver‑assist features that used to be standard on every car are increasingly being unbundled or turned into software‑locked options, and pricing for Full Self‑Driving (FSD) continues to move around as Tesla leans harder into the idea of future robotaxis.

### Key software considerations for 2026 Teslas

What to watch when you compare new and used

#### Autopilot changes

Tesla has pared back which cars ship with features like Autosteer by default and which require paid upgrades. Carefully check the window sticker (new) or software screen (used) for what’s actually enabled.

#### FSD expectations vs reality

FSD remains a Level 2 driver‑assist system that still requires active supervision. Treat it as a comfort and convenience feature, not as a replacement for your attention or insurance.

#### OTA and feature drift

Over‑the‑air (OTA) updates can improve efficiency and usability, but occasional feature removals or changes happen too. When you buy used, make sure the current software behavior matches your expectations.

### Don’t assume driverless capability

Marketing and reality are not the same. No 2026 Tesla you can buy today is a legally driverless robotaxi. You are still responsible for control of the vehicle at all times, no matter which software package you’ve purchased.

## Range, battery and charging: How the 2026 Teslas compare

### Approximate 2026 Tesla range and charging comparison

These are directional ranges and DC fast‑charging capabilities typical of 2026‑era Teslas; specific trims and wheel choices will vary.

| Model | Typical EPA range window | Battery size class | Best‑case DC fast charge | Ideal use case |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Model 3 | ~270–330 mi | Mid‑60s kWh | Up to ~250 kW | Efficient commuting and road trips |
| Model Y | ~260–320 mi | Mid‑70s kWh | Up to ~250 kW | Family crossover, one‑car household |
| Cybertruck | ~250–340 mi+ | Very large pack | High (truck‑specific)','" | Towing, work, adventure use |
| Roadster (claimed) | >600 mi (claimed) | Very large performance | Extremely high (claimed) | Low‑volume halo / track toy |

Always confirm exact ratings and connector details before you buy or road‑trip.

### Battery and charging checklist when shopping a Tesla in 2026

#### 1. Focus on usable range, not just EPA

Look at how far you actually drive in a day and in your worst‑case conditions (winter, highway, loaded). Buying 100 extra miles you never use isn’t efficient, but buying too little range makes ownership stressful.

#### 2. Check battery health on used cars

Range loss is usually modest in the first few years, but heavy fast‑charging or heat can accelerate degradation. Use a third‑party battery health report or tools like the Recharged Score to see real data instead of guessing.

#### 3. Understand the connector landscape

In North America, Tesla’s NACS connector is quickly becoming the standard, and many other automakers are switching over. That makes Teslas convenient to charge but also raises questions about adapter need for older non‑Tesla EVs.

#### 4. Confirm fast‑charge behavior

Not all trims and software versions charge at the same speed. If road trips matter, look for real‑world owner tests, not just peak kW marketing figures.

## Pricing and total cost of ownership in 2026

Tesla’s list prices and incentives have been a moving target for several years, influenced by demand swings, tax‑credit rules and competition. By 2026, you should think in terms of total cost of ownership rather than just the sticker on the website configurator.

- New Model 3 and Model Y pricing in 2026 typically spans from the low‑$40,000s for sensibly optioned base trims into the high‑$50,000s or more for Performance and heavily optioned versions.
- Cybertruck pricing varies widely by configuration and local availability; early production trucks often carry higher effective prices than future, higher‑volume trims.
- Federal and state incentives can meaningfully change the math, but eligibility rules change often, verify credits for the exact VIN and build date you’re considering.
- Insurance, tires and potential FSD software purchases can add thousands of dollars over your ownership period; bake them into your budget, not as afterthoughts.

### Why used Teslas can be a bargain in 2026

Aggressive new‑car price cuts in 2023–2025 compressed residuals. That created a window of opportunity for used‑Tesla buyers in 2026: you can often get a relatively young car with modern hardware at a steep discount versus its original MSRP.

## Buying new vs used in 2026: Where the smart money goes

### When buying new makes sense

- You want the very latest hardware and software features, with full warranty coverage.
- You plan to keep the car a long time and don’t want to think about prior use or unknown charging habits.
- Specific configuration or color matters and you can’t easily find it used.

### When used is the smarter play

- You’re value‑focused and comfortable letting the original buyer eat the steepest depreciation.
- You’re okay with a slightly older infotainment look as long as core range and charging features are solid.
- You can get independent battery‑health data and a clear history instead of guessing.

### Model‑by‑model used opportunities

In 2026, late‑model used Model 3 and Model Y are often the most rational way into the Tesla ecosystem. Used Cybertrucks can make sense if you genuinely need the capability, but they’re more likely to be impulse purchases with unusual usage histories, inspect them carefully.

## How Recharged helps you shop used Teslas with less risk

Buying a used Tesla in 2026 doesn’t have to mean rolling the dice on an opaque battery history or guessing if you’re overpaying. Recharged was built specifically to make used EV ownership simple and transparent, and that applies directly to Model 3, Model Y, Cybertruck and legacy Model S/X shoppers.

Beyond the usual used‑car checklist

## FAQ: Tesla’s 2026 model lineup

### Frequently asked questions about the 2026 Tesla lineup

Which Tesla model should I buy in 2026 if I want the best value?

Is the Tesla Roadster actually available to buy in 2026?

Are Model S and Model X still part of Tesla’s 2026 lineup?

Is it better to get Full Self‑Driving on a new 2026 Tesla or skip it?

How does a 2026 Tesla compare to newer rivals like Hyundai, Kia or Rivian?

Do I need to worry about battery degradation on a 3–5 year old Tesla?

Can I trade my current Tesla for a different model in the 2026 lineup through Recharged?

## Bottom line: Which 2026 Tesla fits you best?

### Match your needs to Tesla’s 2026 lineup

#### Efficiency‑first commuter

Prioritize a Model 3 RWD or Long Range for the best blend of price, range and efficiency.

Skip expensive wheel packages that hurt efficiency; spend on winter tires if you’re in a cold climate.

Buying used? Look for low‑mileage 2022–2025 cars with documented battery health.

#### Family and one‑car household

Start your search with a Model Y Long Range for extra headroom on space and range.

If budget is tight, a used Model Y RWD or base AWD can still work well for suburban duty.

Pay attention to interior wear, tire condition and software options, they matter more in daily use than pure 0–60 numbers.

#### Truck and adventure use

Only consider Cybertruck if you’ll genuinely use its towing, off‑road or cargo capacity.

Plan your routes around high‑power charging locations that can comfortably accommodate a large truck.

If you rarely tow or haul, a Model Y with a hitch may be a calmer, cheaper long‑term choice.

#### Enthusiast and performance buyer

A Model 3 or Model Y Performance gives you track‑day acceleration without exotic‑car running costs.

Keep in mind that big wheels and sticky tires increase consumable costs and can hurt ride quality.

Unless you’re in the 1% shopping genuine supercars, treat the Roadster as a sideshow, not a serious purchase plan.

Tesla’s 2026 lineup isn’t the simple S‑3‑X‑Y story it once was. Instead, it’s a maturing ecosystem centered on the Model 3 and Model Y, with Cybertruck and a still‑mythical Roadster out on the fringes. If you focus on matching your real needs to the right body style, range and budget, and you insist on transparent battery health and fair pricing, you can still make a Tesla the smartest move in your EV journey. And if you’re leaning toward used, Recharged is built to give you the data and support traditional dealerships rarely provide.

Tesla Vehicle Lineup Explained: Every Model in 2026

Close Menu

Subscribe

Follow Us

Share

Tesla’s lineup has gotten smaller, not bigger. Model S and Model X are gone, and the current range comes down to three vehicles, each split into multiple trims with prices that move more often than most car buyers expect.

## TL;DR

- Tesla’s 2026 lineup is three vehicles: Model 3, Model Y, and Cybertruck.
- Model S and Model X ended production entirely in 2026.
- Model 3 starts at $36,990; Model Y starts at $39,990; Cybertruck starts at $69,990.
- The Model Y L is a new three-row variant added in July 2026.
- Full Self-Driving is subscription-only at $99 a month; the one-time purchase ended.

## What does Tesla sell in 2026?

Tesla’s current US lineup is three vehicles: the Model 3 sedan, the Model Y compact SUV, and the Cybertruck pickup. That’s it. There’s no sedan flagship, no full-size SUV, and no entry-level hatchback.

This is a narrower lineup than Tesla has offered at almost any point since 2021. The Model S and Model X, Tesla’s original flagship sedan and SUV, ended production entirely in 2026 as Tesla shifted the Fremont factory toward other priorities, including Optimus robot production.

Anyone shopping for those two models now is shopping for used inventory, not a new order.

Each of the three remaining models comes in several trims, and Tesla changes trim names, prices, and equipment more frequently than traditional automakers. Treat every price below as a snapshot, and check Tesla’s own configurator before ordering.

## Model 3: the sedan

The Model 3 is Tesla’s least expensive model and its only sedan. It comes in four trims for 2026: Standard, Premium Rear-Wheel Drive, Premium All-Wheel Drive, and Performance.

### Model 3 pricing and range

| Trim | MSRP | EPA range | 0-60 mph |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Standard | $36,990 | 363 miles | N/A |
| Premium RWD | $42,490 | 363 miles | N/A |
| Premium AWD | $47,490 | 346 miles | 4.2 sec |
| Performance | $54,990 | 309 miles | 2.9 sec |

The Standard trim returned for 2026 after a one-year absence, and it’s the most affordable Tesla currently sold, giving up some equipment (ventilated seats, the rear-passenger touchscreen, ambient lighting) that the Premium trims include. The Performance trim trades range for a 2.9-second 0-60 time and a 155 mph top speed.

All four trims share the 2024 “Highland” refresh styling: reprofiled bumpers, a rear light bar, and an updated cabin. Prices above are MSRP before the mandatory destination fee and exclude any state incentives.

## Model Y: the compact SUV

The Model Y is Tesla’s best-selling model and, since a 2026 refresh Tesla calls “Juniper,” its most extensively updated one. It now spans six configurations, including a brand-new three-row variant.

### Model Y pricing and range

| Trim | MSRP | EPA range | Seating |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Standard RWD | $39,990 | 321 miles | 5 |
| Standard AWD | $41,990 | 294 miles | 5 |
| Premium RWD | $45,990 | 357 miles | 5 |
| Premium AWD | $49,990 | 327 miles | 5 (7 optional) |
| Performance | $57,990 | 306 miles | 5 |
| Model Y L Launch Series | $61,990 | 320-325 miles (est.) | 6 |

The Juniper refresh brought a redesigned front light bar, better sound insulation, and, on Premium trims and above, an 8-inch rear-seat touchscreen and ventilated front seats.

One change affects every trim: Autopilot’s lane-centering and adaptive cruise features are no longer standard equipment. The hardware ships on every car, but using it now requires a Full Self-Driving subscription.

The Model Y L, added in July 2026, is Tesla’s first three-row Model Y, seating six in a 2+2+2 layout on a stretched wheelbase. It’s currently sold only in the fully-equipped Launch Series trim, with a less expensive standard version expected to follow.

A seven-seat third row is also available as a $2,500 option on the standard-length Premium AWD, the only other Model Y trim that seats more than five.

## Cybertruck: the pickup

credit: https://www.topspeed.com/

The Cybertruck is Tesla’s stainless-steel electric pickup, restructured in February 2026 into a simpler three-trim lineup: a base all-wheel-drive trim, a Premium all-wheel-drive trim, and the tri-motor Cyberbeast.

### Cybertruck pricing and range

| Trim | MSRP | EPA range | 0-60 mph | Max towing |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| All-Wheel Drive | $69,990 | 325 miles | 4.1 sec | 7,500 lbs |
| Premium AWD | $79,990 | 325 miles | 4.1 sec | 11,000 lbs |
| Cyberbeast | $99,990 | 320 miles | 2.6 sec | 11,000 lbs |

Every Cybertruck trim shares the same 123 kWh structural battery pack and can DC fast charge at up to 350 kW, adding roughly 137 miles of range in 15 minutes.

The base AWD trim cuts cost by dropping air suspension, the rear touchscreen, and some interior trim, and by capping tow rating below the Premium and Cyberbeast’s 11,000-pound max.

A single-motor, rear-wheel-drive Cybertruck existed briefly in 2025 before Tesla discontinued it; the lineup has been AWD-and-up ever since.

## What happened to Model S and Model X?

Tesla ended production of both the Model S sedan and Model X SUV in 2026, closing out the two models that launched the company’s shift from a niche automaker to a mass-market one.

Neither has a confirmed successor. Buyers who want one now are shopping the used market, where remaining new inventory has largely sold through.

## Full Self-Driving: what it costs across the lineup

Full Self-Driving (Supervised) is available on every 2026 Tesla, but the one-time purchase option ended February 14, 2026. It’s subscription-only now, at $99 a month in the US, and Tesla has said publicly that price will rise as the software’s capabilities improve. There’s no indication yet of when or by how much.

This applies uniformly across Model 3, Model Y, and Cybertruck. The hardware needed to run FSD ships standard on every trim; the subscription is what activates it.

## Common mistakes when comparing the Tesla lineup

Assuming Model S or Model X are still available to order. They’re not. Any listing offering a “new” Model S or Model X in the US is almost certainly leftover dealer or Tesla-owned inventory, not a fresh factory order.

Comparing MSRP figures without checking the date. Tesla adjusted Model 3 and Model Y pricing multiple times in 2026 alone, including a February-March restructure that changed trim names on both cars. A price you saw last month may already be wrong.

Confusing Autopilot with Full Self-Driving. Since the Model Y’s Juniper refresh, even basic lane-centering requires an FSD subscription on new cars. Don’t assume “Autopilot” still means what it did in past model years.

## Frequently asked questions

### How many models does Tesla currently sell?

Tesla sells three vehicles in the US as of 2026: the Model 3 sedan, Model Y SUV, and Cybertruck pickup.

### Is the Tesla Model S still being made?

No. Tesla ended Model S and Model X production entirely in 2026, and neither has a confirmed replacement.

### What is the cheapest new Tesla you can buy?

The Model 3 Standard, starting at $36,990 MSRP before destination fees and incentives.

### Does Full Self-Driving still cost a one-time fee?

No. Tesla ended the one-time FSD purchase on February 14, 2026. It’s now a $99-a-month subscription across the lineup.

### What is the Model Y L?

It’s a new three-row Model Y variant, added in July 2026, that seats six on a longer wheelbase. It’s currently sold only in a fully-equipped Launch Series trim.

### Does the federal EV tax credit still apply to Tesla vehicles?

No. The federal New Clean Vehicle Credit ended for vehicles acquired after September 30, 2025, so it no longer applies to any new Tesla purchase.

Tesla CEO Elon Musk said the company will stop making two of its car models this year, and repurpose the factory space to make robots instead.

Frederic J. Brown / AFP / Getty Images

Close

### Key Takeaways

- Elon Musk said Tesla would stop making the Model S sedan and Model X SUV later this year, freeing up factory space to make robots.
- The news for now means a smaller lineup of Tesla consumer vehicles—which Musk said was "part of our overall shift to an autonomous future."

Get personalized, AI-powered answers built on 27+ years of trusted expertise.

ASK

Elon Musk wants investors to think of Tesla as more than a car company—and it looks like he means business.

The Tesla (TSLA) CEO on Wednesday said the company would stop producing two of its EV models—the Model S sedan and the Model X small SUV—by the end of the first half of 2026. The change will for now leave the company's consumer lineup with the Model 3 sedan, it's most affordable vehicle at present; the Model Y SUV; and the Cybertruck. (Tesla also alluded to progress on a new high-end Roadster earlier today.)

### Why This Matters to Tesla Investors

Elon Musk expects Tesla to ramp up production of its Optimus robots this year. To do that, he needs factory space—and that led him to decide to stop making two Tesla car models, including its well-known Model S sedan. The decision illustrates his determination to transition the company into much more than a carmaker.

The decision, Musk said during a Wednesday conference call, was "slightly sad. But it is time to bring the S [and] X programs to an end. It's part of our overall shift to an autonomous future." (The call was associated with Tesla's latest results; read more Investopedia coverage of today's Magnificent Seven earnings here.)

Musk is in the process of leading Tesla through a high-stakes—for both him and the company—transition from a carmaker into a business he hopes to position at the forefront of autonomous driving, robotics and artificial intelligence. Its auto deliveries fell year-over-year in 2025, and Musk among other things wants to start producing its Optimus robots at scale this year.

That's part of the reason he's ending the S and X programs: Musk on Wednesday said he would take Fremont., Calif., factory space currently used to make them and repurpose it to make the robots instead.

## Related Education

Elon Musk: Business Icon, Innovator, and Controversial Leader

Magnificent 7 Stocks: What You Need To Know

Musk did say the company will support the S and X "for as long as people have the vehicles." But ending their production has another side effect: The jocular observation that, taken together, one could use the names of four Teslas to spell "S3XY" won't work for much longer.

In the meantime, you can still buy the Teslas that will soon be American automotive history. The company's web site shows the S starting at around $95,000 and the X at close to six figures. The Model 3 starts at about $35,000.

"We’re really moving into a future that is based on autonomy," Musk said. "So if you’re interested in buying a Model S and X, now would be the time to order it."

# Tesla

Tesla is an electric-car company based in Palo Alto, Calif. The beneficiary of excellent timing, Tesla effectively was the only company building battery-electric cars when fuel prices spiked in the summer of 2008; as a result, no news story on alternative fuels was complete without mentioning the marque. Since then, the company has expanded from car-building to making energy-related products like solar roof panels and energy storage systems. It also has a global network of more than 75,000 Supercharger fast-charging stations; these were previously exclusive to Tesla drivers, but Tesla has opened up access to most other automakers so non-Tesla EVs can use them.

Tesla’s current vehicles include the Model 3 compact sedan, Model S mid-size luxury sedan, Model X luxury SUV and Model Y compact SUV. The most recent addition is the new-for-2024 Cybertruck, an extremely angular pickup truck with stainless-steel body panels and an available tri-motor powertrain that makes up to 845 horsepower.

# Tesla

How we rank cars

What started as a little company in California has shifted the way people think about electric vehicles, from practical economy cars to aspirational performance machines. Tesla's portfolio is impressive and only expanding, with the large Model S hatchback, compact Model 3 sedan, Model X three-row crossover, and the Model Y compact crossover.

Least Expensive : The Model 3 serves as the entry point to the Tesla sedan lineup with a starting price around $48,000. The entry point to the Tesla SUV lineup isn't quite as low; the Model Y starts just over $67,000.

Sportiest : Until the Roadster finally arrives, the Tesla Model S Plaid+ is the brand's highest performance model. With 0-60 mph dispatched in a claimed 2.0 seconds, it's quick enough to out-accelerate almost everything on the road.

Most Popular : In keeping with the market's crossover-hungry appetite, the Tesla Model Y is the brand's most popular model. The Model 3 is also popular for anyone seeking a good, premium four-door.

Most Expensive : Packing an incredible 1,020 horsepower, the Tesla Model X Plaid has a starting price around $140,000.
